sentences.text: The genus name Volia comes from Voli Voli Cave, and the species name honors archaeologist Atholl Anderson.
Volia was approximately 2 to 3 meters long, making it the largest predator and likely apex predator of Pleistocene Fiji.
Researchers estimated Volia's size by comparing its preserved femur to that of a saltwater crocodile, suggesting a length of 2 to 3 meters.
The genus Volia was described by Molnar, Worthy, and Willis in 2002.
Fossils of Volia were discovered by Trevor Worthy and Atholl Anderson in 1997 and 1998.
The holotype of Volia was found in Wainibuku Cave, while the largest fossils came from Voli Voli Cave.
The holotype of Volia is housed at the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa.
Volia likely fed on giant iguanas, flightless birds, or fish.
Volia may have been more terrestrial than modern crocodiles.
The hinge-like joint motion of the distal ulnare suggests Volia was better adapted to move on land than modern saltwater crocodiles.
Volia is an extinct genus containing only one species and is a mekosuchine crocodylian related to Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus.
Early phylogenetic studies suggested Volia was the sister taxon to Mekosuchus, with Trilophosuchus being more basal and Quinkana in a polytomy.
Volia lived during the Pleistocene and possibly the Holocene.
Fossils of Volia have been found in caves on Viti Levu and the island of Naigani in Fiji.
Volia lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
Fossil material tentatively assigned to Volia from Naigani dates to the Holocene, around 2,900 to 2,700 years ago.
It is debated whether humans caused the extinction of Volia, as remains found in Lapita culture ovens could also belong to modern saltwater crocodiles.
